slides.title: Ancient Greece Day
slides.subtitle: Dress up. Build a temple. Compete in the Olympics. Vote like an Athenian. Share a Greek feast.
slides.strap: Date: to be confirmed. Costumes on from the start of the day.

slides.title: Why Ancient Greece?
slides.intro: About 2,500 years ago the Greeks lived in small city-states around the Aegean Sea. Their ideas still shape our lives today.

facts.head: City-states
facts.text: Athens, Sparta, Corinth and Thebes each ruled themselves. They traded, argued and sometimes fought.

facts.head: Democracy
facts.text: Athenians invented a system where citizens voted on the laws. Our word democracy comes from Greek: demos (people) and kratos (power).

facts.head: The Olympics
facts.text: Athletes from across Greece met at Olympia every four years to compete in honour of Zeus.

facts.head: Temples and art
facts.text: Marble temples with tall columns, painted pottery and carved statues. The Parthenon still stands in Athens.

facts.head: Theatre, myths and ideas
facts.text: Plays with masks, stories of gods and heroes, and thinkers such as Socrates, Plato and Aristotle.

facts.head: The alphabet
facts.text: Our word alphabet comes from the first two Greek letters: alpha and beta.

slides.title: The day at a glance
slides.intro: Six parts. You take part in all of them. Times may shift a little on the day.

slides.title: Dress up: who will you be?
slides.intro: Nothing needs to be bought. Most costumes start with an old white sheet, a pillowcase or a plain T-shirt. Wear your PE kit underneath for the Olympics.

characters.name: Athenian citizen
characters.kit: Long chiton (sheet or pillowcase), cord belt, himation wrap over one shoulder, sandals.

characters.name: Spartan hoplite
characters.kit: Short tunic, red cloak (red fabric or towel), card helmet, round card shield with a lambda.

characters.name: Olympic athlete
characters.kit: Knee-length tunic over PE kit, cord belt, olive wreath made from card leaves.

characters.name: Goddess Athena
characters.kit: Long peplos, gold card helmet, small owl, a shield or a spear made of rolled paper.

characters.name: Philosopher or potter
characters.kit: Chiton and himation, a scroll made of paper, or an apron and a paper-plate pot.

slides.title: How to make a chiton in five minutes
slides.intro: The chiton was the everyday tunic for men, women and children. It is one rectangle of cloth, pinned and belted. The Greeks dyed theirs in bright colours, so white is not the only option.

steps.head: 1. Fold
steps.text: Take a single sheet or a large pillowcase. Fold it in half so the fold sits under one arm.

steps.head: 2. Pin
steps.text: Pin the top edge at both shoulders with safety pins or two large buttons. Leave a gap for your head.

steps.head: 3. Belt
steps.text: Tie a cord, dressing gown belt or ribbon round the waist. Pull the cloth up so the hem clears your ankles.

steps.head: 4. Finish
steps.text: Add a himation (a second piece of cloth over one shoulder), sandals or trainers, and a card leaf wreath.

rules: No metal, sharp or pointed props. Card shields and paper spears are fine.
Trainers on for the Olympics. Hair tied back.

slides.title: Temples: homes for the gods
slides.intro: A Greek temple was not for worshippers to sit in. It was a house for a statue of a god. The Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens was built for Athena between 447 and 432 BC.

points.head: Pediment
points.text: The triangle at the top, filled with carved statues of gods and heroes.

points.head: Frieze with metopes
points.text: A band of carved panels running above the columns. The Parthenon had 92 metopes.

points.head: Columns
points.text: Doric columns, 8 across the front and 17 down each side. 46 on the outside in total.

points.head: Steps
points.text: Three marble steps lead up to the platform the temple stands on.

points.head: Marble
points.text: Cut from Mount Pentelicus, about 16 km away, and hauled up the hill by oxen.

slides.title: Three kinds of column
slides.intro: Spot the capital, the carved top of the column. It tells you which order the temple belongs to. You will choose one for your own temple.

points.head: Doric
points.text: Plain, sturdy and the oldest. A flat square capital and no base. The Parthenon uses Doric.

points.head: Ionic
points.text: Slimmer with a scroll shape (volutes) on the capital and a stepped base. Found on the Erechtheion.

points.head: Corinthian
points.text: The most decorated. Carved acanthus leaves on the capital. Later copied all over the Roman Empire.

slides.title: Temple art exhibition
slides.intro: In the morning workshop you create one piece for our class exhibition. Parents and other classes visit the gallery walk at the end of the day.

cards.head: Temple model
cards.text: Card box base, paper-tube or rolled-card columns, a card pediment. Choose Doric, Ionic or Corinthian capitals.
cards.note: Bring in tubes and small boxes from home this week.

cards.head: Frieze panel
cards.text: Draw a metope scene on a strip of card: an Olympic event, a myth or a procession. Use the side-on figures seen on Greek pottery.
cards.note: Pencil first, then black and terracotta.

cards.head: Greek pot
cards.text: Design an amphora or kylix on a paper plate or card shape. Black-figure or red-figure style with a meander border.

cards.head: Curator card
cards.text: Every piece needs a label: title, artist, order of column or style, and one sentence on what it shows.

success: Columns stand straight and evenly spaced.
A pediment or capital shows the order you chose.
Decoration uses Greek patterns and side-on figures.
A finished curator card sits beside the piece.

slides.title: The Ancient Olympic Games
slides.intro: The first recorded Games were held at Olympia in 776 BC. They ran every four years for more than a thousand years.

facts.head: For Zeus
facts.text: The Games were a religious festival. A huge statue of Zeus stood in his temple at Olympia.

facts.head: Only Greeks
facts.text: Free Greek men travelled from every city-state. Women had their own games at Olympia, the Heraia.

facts.head: The truce
facts.text: Wars stopped so that athletes and visitors could travel safely to the Games.

facts.head: The prize
facts.text: No medals. The winner received a wreath of olive leaves and a hero's welcome at home.

facts.head: The stadion
facts.text: The oldest event was a sprint of about 192 metres, the length of the stadium.

facts.head: The pentathlon
facts.text: Five events in one day: running, long jump, discus, javelin and wrestling.

slides.title: Olympic events to try out for
slides.intro: Try-outs in the first 20 minutes. Everyone competes in at least two events for their city-state. Points for first, second and third.

events.name: Stadion sprint
events.then: A straight sprint of one stade, about 192 m.
events.now: Playground sprint, heats then a final.

events.name: Long jump
events.then: A standing jump swinging stone weights called halteres.
events.now: Standing jump holding two beanbags. Furthest jump wins.

events.name: Discus
events.then: A heavy bronze or stone disc thrown for distance.
events.now: Foam frisbee or paper plate throw. Distance and accuracy.

events.name: Javelin
events.then: A light spear thrown with a leather loop for extra spin.
events.now: Foam pool-noodle javelin into a target zone.

events.name: Chariot race
events.then: Four-horse chariots racing round the hippodrome.
events.now: Hoop relay in teams of four. Hold the hoop, round the cone, hand over.

events.name: Hoplite race
events.then: Running in armour carrying a shield and helmet.
events.now: Obstacle course carrying a card shield. Drop it and you restart that section.

slides.title: How the Games will run
slides.intro: You compete for a city-state, not just for yourself. Teams are mixed from across the class.

Make a team chant and a team flag before break

Team captains and teachers agree who goes where.

slides.title: Vote like an Athenian
slides.intro: From 508 BC Athens was a democracy. Citizens met on a hill called the Pnyx up to 40 times a year to argue and vote. We will hold our own Assembly after lunch.

facts.head: The Assembly (Ekklesia)
facts.text: Any male citizen over 18 could speak and vote. About 6,000 came to big meetings. Voting was usually by a show of hands.

facts.head: The Council of 500
facts.text: Chosen by lot using a machine called a kleroterion, so rich and poor had the same chance.

facts.head: Ostracism
facts.text: Once a year citizens could scratch a name on a broken piece of pottery, an ostrakon. With 6,000 votes that person left Athens for ten years.

facts.head: Who was left out?
facts.text: Women, enslaved people and foreigners could not vote. Was it really fair? We will debate this.

agenda: Motion 1: Which city-state should host next year's Games?
Motion 2: Which temple deserves the Exhibition Prize?
Speakers hold the speaker's staff. Vote by show of hands, then pebbles in the pot for a secret ballot.

slides.title: The Greek feast
slides.intro: Ancient Greeks ate simply: bread, olives, cheese, fruit, beans and fish. Meat was for festivals. Everything on our table is vegetarian so that everyone can share.

then.head: Bread and barley
then.text: Flat loaves dipped in olive oil.

then.head: Olives and oil
then.text: Grown everywhere. Oil was also used for lamps and skin.

then.head: Fish
then.text: Fresh from the Aegean for those near the coast.

slides.allergy: Allergies and dietary needs: every dish is labelled with its ingredients. The table is vegetarian and contains dairy, gluten and sesame. Tell your teacher about any allergy before the day.

slides.title: And more
slides.intro: Short activities running through the day, between the big events.

cards.head: Your name in Greek
cards.text: Write your name using the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet and pin it to your costume.

cards.head: Theatre masks
cards.text: Comedy or tragedy? Make a card mask like the actors in the Theatre of Dionysus.
cards.note: Big expressions so the back row can see.

cards.head: Myth corner
cards.text: Hear the stories of Theseus and the Minotaur, Perseus and Medusa, and the Trojan Horse.
cards.note: Retell one in a six-panel frieze.

cards.head: Pottery patterns
cards.text: Learn the meander (Greek key) and the wave border and use them on your exhibition piece.
cards.note: Draw it with a ruler first.

slides.title: What to bring
slides.intro: Check this list the night before. Everything should be named.

items.head: Your costume
items.text: Worn to school over your PE kit. Chiton, belt and any card props.

items.head: Trainers
items.text: On your feet or in a bag. Sandals are fine for the parade, not for the Games.

items.head: Hair bobble
items.text: Long hair tied back for the events.

items.head: Temple materials
items.text: Cardboard tubes, small boxes and lids. Bring them in during the week before, not on the day.

items.head: Feast contribution (optional)
items.text: One item from the feast list, shop-bought and in its packet so the ingredients can be read. Nothing containing nuts.

items.head: Your two Olympic choices
items.text: Decide which events you want to try out for and tell your team captain.

items.head: A big smile
items.text: You will be in the class photo in costume at 8:50.

slides.footer: Leave at home: anything metal, sharp or pointed, bought weapons, glass, nuts and anything you would be sad to lose.
